Bhatti Neutral Citation No. 2024:Mphc-Jbp:44422 1 In The High Court Of Madhya Pradesh At Jabalpur Before Hon'Ble Shri Justice Maninder S. Bhatti On The 3 rd Of September, 2024 Criminal Revision No. 1811 of 2024 Raman Yadav Versus The State Of Madhya Pradesh Appearance: Order This Revision arises out of an order dated 1.3.2024, passed by the Appellate Authority, constituted in terms of Section 70 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (hereinafter referred to as "Act of 2006 for the sake of brevity), dismissing an application filed by present petitioner under Section 5 of the Limitation Act. 2.
texts.facts: Order This Revision arises out of an order dated 1.3.2024, passed by the Appellate Authority, constituted in terms of Section 70 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (hereinafter referred to as "Act of 2006 for the sake of brevity), dismissing an application filed by present petitioner under Section 5 of the Limitation Act. 2. Counsel for the petitioner contends that the order passed by the Adjudicating Authority was assailed by filing an appeal before the Tribunal, which is constituted in terms of Section 70 of the Act of 2006, known as Food Safety Appellate Tribunal. The appeal was filed along with an application filed under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, inasmuch as, the original order dated 17.4.2023 came to the notice of the present petitioner on 8.6.2023. Therefore, delay which had occasioned in filing of the appeal was inadvertent and bona fide . However, the Appellate Authority has proceeded to dismiss the application filed under Section 5 of the Limitation Act and as NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2024:MPHC-JBP:44422 2 CRR-1811-2024 a consequence thereof the appeal itself has been dismissed.
texts.arguments: 3. Counsel for the petitioner contends that the delay was bona fide and inadvertent and the reasons for delay had been duly explained in the application filed under Section 5 of the Limitation Act. The Trial Court ought to have taken recourse to a lenient approach while dealing with the application Raman Yadav vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 3 September, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/133744458/ 1 filed under Section 5 of the Limitation Act as the delay was not inordinate and, therefore, considering the reasons assigned in the application the delay ought to have been condoned. 4. Counsel for the State has supported the order passed by the Appellate Authority and it is contended that the order does not require any interference. The Apex Court in the case of N. Balakrishnan vs. M. Krishnamurthy (1998) 7 SCC 123 in para 10 and 11 has held as under : "10. The reason for such a different stance is thus: The primary function of a court is to adjudicate the dispute between the parties and to advance substantial justice. The time- limit fixed for approaching the court in different situations is not because on the expiry of such time a bad cause would transform into a good cause. 11. Rules of limitation are not meant to destroy the rights of parties. They are meant to see that parties do not resort to dilatory tactics, but seek their remedy promptly. The object of providing a legal remedy is to repair the damage caused by reason of legal injury. The law of limitation fixes a lifespan for such legal remedy for the redress of the legal injury so suffered. It is Raman Yadav vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 3 September, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/133744458/ 2 enshrined in the maxim interest reipublicae up sit finis litium (it is for the general welfare that a period be put to litigation). Rules of limitation are not meant to destroy the rights of the parties. The idea is that every legal remedy must be kept alive for a legislatively fixed period of time." 7 .
